pairs.cause: People learned to farm crops and domesticate animals.
pairs.effect: Communities settled in permanent villages instead of migrating.
pairs.explanation: A reliable food supply meant groups no longer had to follow wild herds and plants, so they could stay in one place.

pairs.cause: Farming produced a surplus of food.
pairs.effect: Some people could specialize in jobs besides finding food, like crafts, trade, and religion.
pairs.explanation: Extra food freed part of the population from farming, allowing job specialization — a foundation of civilization.

pairs.cause: Villages stored surplus food and goods.
pairs.effect: Social classes and organized government developed.
pairs.explanation: Deciding who controlled stored wealth led to leaders, rules, and ranked social classes.

pairs.cause: Communities needed to track land, trade, and surplus.
pairs.effect: Early writing and record-keeping systems were invented.
pairs.explanation: Managing a complex settled economy pushed people to record information, leading to the first writing.

pairs.cause: People lived close together with animals in denser settlements.
pairs.effect: Communicable diseases spread more easily among humans.
pairs.explanation: Crowding and contact with domesticated animals created new paths for disease.

pairs.cause: A steadier food supply could support more children.
pairs.explanation: Farming supported far more people per acre than hunting and gathering.

pairs.cause: Settled farmers wanted to protect stored food and fields.
pairs.effect: Communities built permanent walls and defenses.
pairs.explanation: Having wealth worth taking made raids a threat, so villages fortified themselves.
